case_analysis.focal_point: Whether FIFRA preempts a Missouri common-law failure-to-warn claim seeking a cancer warning for an EPA-registered pesticide label when EPA has determined that warning is not required and the manufacturer cannot add it without EPA approval.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), 7 U.S.C. § 136 et seq., especially the express preemption provision barring states from imposing labeling/packaging requirements “in addition to or different from” federal requirements (7 U.S.C. § 136v(b)) and FIFRA’s misbranding/registration/label-approval framework.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Monsanto argues the state-law failure-to-warn verdict is expressly preempted (and effectively also conflict/impossibility preempted) because a tort duty to add a glyphosate cancer warning would impose a state “labeling requirement” that is “in addition to” FIFRA’s requirements, where EPA has reviewed the relevant risk information, determined such a cancer warning is not required (and in some formulations would render the label misleading/misbranded), and the registrant cannot unilaterally add that warning without prior EPA approval. In Monsanto’s view, allowing juries to require warnings that EPA has affirmatively deemed unnecessary (or misleading) would defeat FIFRA’s goal of nationally uniform labeling and create a patchwork of state-by-state label mandates imposed through damages actions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Durnell argues FIFRA does not preempt because the Missouri failure-to-warn claim parallels, rather than adds to, FIFRA’s core prohibition on “misbranding” (i.e., the state claim is framed as enforcing the same duty not to sell a misbranded product), and EPA registration/periodic review is not a binding, preemptive determination that no additional warning could ever be required. Respondent contends that EPA’s decision not to require a cancer warning is not the sort of federal “requirement” that triggers § 136v(b) preemption and that manufacturers can seek EPA approval for stronger warnings (so compliance with both federal and state law is not impossible). Respondent also presses a separation-of-powers/delegation concern: absent clear statutory text, EPA’s informal or non-rulemaking judgments should not be treated as having preemptive force, particularly in the post-Loper Bright environment.
key_precedents: Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. v. Albrecht (2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best counterpoint: EPA’s having “not required” a warning is not necessarily a binding federal prohibition, and Wyeth/Albrecht caution against finding preemption absent clear evidence the warning was legally unavailable. But this case sits in FIFRA’s express-preemption clause, § 136v(b), and as Justice Kagan emphasizes, the only surviving space under Bates is a genuinely parallel state duty; a Missouri verdict compelling a cancer warning after EPA has affirmatively evaluated carcinogenicity and indicated the warning could be misleading under FIFRA’s misbranding framework is not meaningfully “parallel.” Albrecht matters here not to broaden preemption, but to support a narrow, court-determined inquiry: preemption attaches only where the record shows EPA actually exercised its labeling authority on the specific warning and the registrant lacked a lawful unilateral path to add it. That limited approach answers Justice Jackson’s concern about collapsing Bates while still giving effect to Congress’s uniformity command in § 136v(b).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s best point is that EPA’s “not required” position may lack the force of a binding federal prohibition, and Wyeth/Albrecht require “clear evidence” before finding preemption. But this case is governed foremost by FIFRA’s express text: § 136v(b) preempts any state “requirement for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and under Bates a common-law damages verdict is a “requirement” when it effectively compels different label content. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis that the registrant cannot lawfully add the demanded warning unilaterally under FIFRA’s label-approval regime confirms that Missouri’s duty operates as an additional labeling mandate rather than a genuinely parallel misbranding claim. Wyeth and Albrecht, addressing different statutory schemes and implied preemption frameworks, cannot override Congress’s express choice to secure nationally uniform pesticide labeling through § 136v(b).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that EPA’s “not required” statements and registration actions may lack the sort of binding, rule-like character that Wyeth and Albrecht describe when they demand “clear evidence” a stronger warning was legally unavailable. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, this case is anchored in FIFRA’s express-preemption text: § 136v(b) bars any state “requirements for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal ones, and under Bates a tort verdict compelling new label content is itself a prohibited “requirement” unless it is genuinely parallel to federal misbranding. Here EPA did not merely stay silent; it affirmatively evaluated the cancer-warning question within FIFRA’s misbranding framework and indicated such a warning could be misleading—so Missouri’s duty is not enforcing the same federal standard as administered, it is demanding a different label outcome. Wyeth/Albrecht’s implied-preemption caution cannot be used to dilute Congress’s express uniformity clause or to empower state juries to countermand EPA’s considered labeling judgments under FIFRA.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow proposed rule is the most serious challenge because it tries to tie preemption to an “affirmative EPA no-warning/misbranding determination,” but I do not think the record described—registration plus agency letters/guidance expressing that a cancer warning is “not required” and might be misleading—amounts to a federal “requirement” with the force of law that the warning must not appear. Under Bates, the dispositive question is whether the state duty can be understood as enforcing the same misbranding norm (avoid misleading labeling by warning of a material risk), and Wyeth and Merck/Albrecht counsel against treating nonbinding agency views as making a stronger warning legally unavailable absent clear evidence of a lawful federal prohibition. Justice Kagan’s point that a contrary verdict is “hard to characterize as parallel” assumes EPA has conclusively and legally resolved the scientific dispute for all purposes, but FIFRA’s misbranding standard is broad and tort law can operate as a traditional enforcement mechanism where federal law has not clearly foreclosed the warning. Given the real-world stakes and Congress’s choice not to create a tort-free zone, I would not extend § 136v(b) to preempt without a clearer, binding federal action rejecting the specific warning.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s best point is that EPA’s failure to require a warning (or informal communications) should not be treated as a binding federal “requirement” that forbids one, given Wyeth/Albrecht’s insistence on clear evidence and wariness of preemptive “silence.” But Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower framing answers that concern: on this record EPA did not merely refrain—it affirmatively evaluated the carcinogenicity question under FIFRA’s misbranding standard and indicated a glyphosate cancer warning could render the label misleading, and the registrant lacks a lawful unilateral route to add the demanded warning within FIFRA’s approval regime. That makes Missouri’s tort verdict hard to characterize as “parallel” under Bates; it functions as a de facto additional labeling command “in addition to or different from” the federal determination Congress sought to keep uniform in § 136v(b). I would keep the holding tightly tied to an affirmative EPA no-warning/misbranding determination (not mere inaction), which preserves Bates’s parallel-claim space while respecting the statutory text and workable administration.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press that EPA’s “not required” posture lacks the force of law, and Wyeth/Albrecht demand “clear evidence” that the stronger warning was legally unavailable. But this case begins with FIFRA’s express text—§ 136v(b) bars any state “requirements for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal ones—and under Bates a damages verdict that effectively compels new label language is itself such a “requirement.” Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower approach is persuasive: preemption should attach only where the record shows EPA actually engaged the specific warning and, applying the misbranding standard, approved a label without it while indicating the proposed warning could be misleading—making the state duty not “parallel” but different in outcome and therefore preempted. Wyeth/Albrecht do not defeat that conclusion because they address implied conflict preemption in a different statutory structure, whereas here Congress expressly demanded uniform labeling and routed label changes through EPA’s approval regime.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson fairly press that EPA’s saying a warning is “not required” is not automatically a binding federal prohibition, and Wyeth/Albrecht caution against finding preemption without clear evidence the warning was legally unavailable. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, this case principally runs through FIFRA’s express preemption clause, § 136v(b): a state-law damages duty that would, in operation, compel a glyphosate cancer warning after EPA has affirmatively evaluated the issue and indicated such a warning could itself be misleading is a state “requirement … in addition to or different from” the federal labeling determination, not a genuinely “parallel” misbranding claim under Bates. Albrecht’s allocation of the ultimate preemption question to courts supports a narrow, institutional holding tied to an affirmative EPA no-warning/misbranding determination and the registrant’s lack of lawful unilateral means to add the warning. Under my precedent- and text-focused approach, allowing juries to override EPA’s considered label-content judgment would undermine the national uniformity Congress built into § 136v(b).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—echoed by Justice Jackson—is that EPA’s “not required” position may not itself be a binding federal prohibition, and that Wyeth and Albrecht demand “clear evidence” before finding the stronger warning legally unavailable. But the controlling feature here, as Justice Thomas emphasizes, is FIFRA’s express text: § 136v(b) preempts state “requirements for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates recognizes that common-law damages duties can qualify as such requirements when they effectively compel label changes. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s narrower framing persuades me that this record is not about agency silence: EPA affirmatively evaluated the carcinogenicity issue and indicated the proposed cancer warning would be misleading/misbranding under FIFRA as EPA administers it, so Missouri’s duty is not “equivalent to, and fully consistent with,” the federal misbranding standard. On that understanding, Wyeth/Albrecht (implied-preemption in different statutory settings) do not override Congress’s express uniformity clause or Bates’s limitation to genuinely parallel claims.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that a damages verdict can functionally operate as a labeling “requirement,” and Bates acknowledges that practical reality; but Bates also preserves state claims that genuinely parallel FIFRA’s misbranding duties, and I do not think EPA’s registration posture or “not required/potentially misleading” communications—absent a binding, lawmaking action directed at the specific warning—automatically convert federal policy into a prohibitory “requirement” that preempts tort enforcement. Justice Thomas’s text-focused reading of § 136v(b) is powerful, yet if we treat nonbinding agency views as preemptive “requirements,” we risk collapsing Bates’s parallel-claim carveout and displacing traditional tort accountability without the procedural safeguards that accompany clear federal commands. Wyeth and Albrecht matter here not as a wholesale transplant, but as a caution that preemption should turn on “clear evidence” of legal unavailability, not on EPA’s discretionary judgments or litigation positions that do not carry the force of law. On this record, Missouri can still be understood as enforcing a non-misleading-label norm rather than imposing an “in addition to” mandate, and I would not extend § 136v(b) to foreclose that absent a clearer federal prohibition.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 136v(b) expressly bars States from imposing any “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s, and Bates v. Dow Agrosciences confirms that common-law failure-to-warn duties enforced through damages verdicts are “requirements” for labeling. Whatever room Bates left for “parallel” state duties equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding standard, a Missouri verdict compelling a glyphosate cancer warning after EPA has affirmatively determined such a warning is not required—and would be misleading under FIFRA’s misbranding framework—functions as an additional state labeling requirement rather than a truly equivalent one. This is reinforced by the practical impossibility problem identified in PLIVA v. Mensing and Merck v. Albrecht: if the manufacturer cannot unilaterally add the warning without EPA approval, the state-law duty operates as a direct obstacle to the federal labeling regime and the congressional objective of national uniformity embedded in § 136v(b). A narrow holding confined to situations where EPA has made a considered no-warning determination and label changes require prior federal approval best respects precedent while preserving FIFRA’s uniform-labeling structure.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: FIFRA’s text expressly preempts any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and a Missouri common-law failure-to-warn verdict functions as a state-imposed “requirement” because it compels a label change on pain of damages. Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, state-law duties survive only if they are genuinely “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding standard; but where EPA has affirmatively determined a glyphosate cancer warning is not required (and may render the label misleading), a state-law mandate to add that warning is necessarily “in addition to or different from” the federal labeling determination. Because FIFRA centralizes label approval in EPA’s registration/misbranding scheme, allowing juries to impose contrary cancer-warning obligations would defeat the uniformity Congress chose in § 136v(b), and the manufacturer’s inability to add the warning without EPA approval underscores the conflict. Precedent inconsistent with this text-driven result should yield to the statute’s original public meaning and Congress’s decision to vest label content control in the federal regulator rather than state tort law.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: FIFRA’s express “Uniformity” clause, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), bars States from imposing any labeling requirements “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and a Missouri failure-to-warn verdict functionally compels a cancer warning on an EPA-registered label—i.e., a state “requirement for labeling.” Bates v. Dow Agrosciences confirms that common-law failure-to-warn duties are “requirements for labeling,” and its narrow ‘parallel misbranding duty’ carveout applies only when the state duty is “equivalent to, and fully consistent with,” FIFRA’s misbranding regime—not when EPA has affirmatively evaluated the risk information and concluded the cancer warning is not required (and may be misleading). Where the registrant cannot unilaterally change the label and must obtain EPA approval, allowing juries to impose additional warnings would undermine FIFRA’s nationally uniform labeling scheme and raise the same practical impossibility concerns reflected in PLIVA v. Mensing and Merck v. Albrecht’s focus on whether federal law leaves the manufacturer lawful room to add the warning. The better reading is that the state-law duty here is “in addition to” the federally approved label and therefore preempted under § 136v(b).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), bars only state labeling requirements “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences a state common-law failure-to-warn claim survives if it is equivalent to and fully consistent with FIFRA’s misbranding prohibition. EPA’s registration and its view that a cancer warning is “not required” do not, without more, establish a binding federal labeling “requirement” that affirmatively forbids the warning or gives it automatic preemptive force, especially where the statute contemplates label amendments upon EPA approval rather than insulating registrants from tort duties. Consistent with Wyeth v. Levine and Merck v. Albrecht, preemption would require clear evidence that federal law made the stronger warning unlawful; on this record, the manufacturer can seek EPA approval and the State’s duty can operate as a parallel means of enforcing the federal misbranding standard rather than adding a different one.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and Bates holds that common-law failure-to-warn duties can be “requirements for labeling” while permitting only truly “parallel” claims. Here, the Missouri verdict functionally compels a cancer warning that EPA has considered and declined to require—and, on this record, EPA has indicated such a warning could render the product misbranded—so the state duty is not parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding standard as administered through EPA’s label-approval regime. Given that registrants cannot unilaterally add the demanded warning without EPA approval, the claim also presses toward the Mensing/Albrecht line’s practical impossibility logic, reinforcing that this damages action would impose an additional state labeling mandate inconsistent with FIFRA’s uniformity design. Treating a jury’s contrary warning mandate as “parallel” would defeat § 136v(b)’s textual bar and invite the very patchwork FIFRA’s labeling framework is structured to avoid.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: FIFRA expressly preempts any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and Bates confirms that common-law failure-to-warn duties can qualify as such “requirements” when they would compel different label content. Here, EPA has exercised its statutory authority to apply FIFRA’s misbranding standard, 7 U.S.C. § 136(q)(1)(G), and determined a glyphosate cancer warning is not required (and, on this record, would risk rendering the label misleading), so a Missouri verdict demanding that warning would impose a non-parallel, additional labeling requirement. Allowing juries to mandate warnings EPA has rejected would defeat FIFRA’s textual commitment to nationally uniform labeling and would effectively let state tort law override federal label-approval judgments in an area Congress reserved to EPA. Whatever room Bates leaves for “parallel” claims, it does not extend to a claim that, in operation, requires a label change the federal scheme does not require and the registrant cannot make unilaterally without EPA approval.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: FIFRA expressly preempts any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences common-law failure-to-warn duties count as such “requirements.” While Bates preserved state claims that are genuinely “equivalent to, and fully consistent with” FIFRA’s misbranding standard, a Missouri verdict effectively compelling a glyphosate cancer warning that EPA has determined is not required (and that EPA has indicated could render the label misleading) imposes an additional state-law labeling requirement rather than a parallel one. Practical workability and national uniformity—the very purpose of § 136v(b)’s “Uniformity” provision—counsel against allowing juries to override EPA’s label determinations and create a patchwork of de facto state label mandates through damages actions. Consistent with Mensing and Albrecht’s focus on whether federal law leaves the manufacturer with lawful unilateral means to add the warning, the record here indicates the registrant cannot add the warning without EPA approval, reinforcing preemption in these circumstances.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and Bates confirms that common-law failure-to-warn duties can qualify as such “requirements.” Under Bates, a state claim survives only if it is genuinely “equivalent to, and fully consistent with,” FIFRA’s misbranding standards; here, the Missouri verdict effectively compels a cancer warning that EPA has affirmatively determined is not required and, in relevant respects, would render the label misleading/misbranded, so the state duty is not “parallel” but “in addition to” the federal labeling determination. Given FIFRA’s label-approval framework (and the record premise that the registrant cannot add this warning without EPA approval), the tort duty functions as a prohibited state labeling mandate, paralleling the impossibility reasoning of PLIVA v. Mensing when a regulated entity cannot unilaterally change the federally governed label. Precedent sensitivity cuts toward preemption because allowing juries to impose warnings EPA has disallowed would defeat § 136v(b)’s uniformity command and collapse Bates’s narrow “equivalent” carveout into a general anti-preemption rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under FIFRA’s express preemption clause, § 136v(b) bars state “requirements for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, but Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC holds that common-law failure-to-warn duties are preempted only when they are non-parallel—i.e., not genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding standard. Here, EPA registration and periodic review, without a binding federal prohibition on adding the warning, do not themselves establish a federal “requirement” that no cancer warning may appear, and Missouri’s claim can be understood as enforcing the same core duty not to market a “misbranded” product. Consistent with Wyeth v. Levine and Merck v. Albrecht, preemption would require clear evidence that federal law made the warning legally unavailable (not merely that EPA previously did not require it), and the record as framed leaves room for the manufacturer to seek EPA approval rather than treating EPA’s non-rulemaking judgments as categorically preemptive. Given procedural-fairness and federalism concerns, I would not extend § 136v(b) to immunize a defendant from traditional tort accountability absent an unmistakable, legally binding federal determination forbidding the warning.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether FIFRA expressly and/or impliedly preempts a state-law failure-to-warn verdict demanding a cancer warning for an EPA-registered pesticide label when EPA has determined that such a warning is not required and the manufacturer cannot add it without EPA approval.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), 7 U.S.C. § 136 et seq., especially the express preemption clause (commonly codified at 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b)) barring States from imposing “any requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s requirements; and FIFRA’s misbranding/registration and label-approval scheme administered by EPA.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Monsanto argues that Durnell’s state-law failure-to-warn claim is preempted because (1) FIFRA expressly bars state “requirements” that would force a label warning “in addition to or different from” EPA-approved labeling; (2) EPA has repeatedly evaluated glyphosate/carcinogenicity and determined that a cancer warning is not required (and, per EPA’s position, would render the product misbranded), so the Missouri verdict effectively overrides a federal regulatory judgment; and (3) it is, as a practical and legal matter, impossible to comply with both federal law (which requires EPA approval before adding/altering hazard warnings and treats unapproved or misleading warnings as misbranding) and the state-law duty that the verdict enforces. Monsanto and supporting amici emphasize the need for national uniformity in pesticide labeling and contend that allowing juries to impose warning duties that EPA rejected converts tort law into an alternative labeling regulator, undermining FIFRA’s uniform federal scheme.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Durnell argues that his failure-to-warn claim is not preempted because FIFRA’s express preemption provision, as interpreted in Bates, leaves room for state tort suits that parallel (rather than add to) FIFRA’s misbranding standard—i.e., state law can enforce a duty not to sell a “misbranded” product whose labeling is allegedly misleading/inadequate. He contends that EPA registration/label approval does not create binding federal ‘requirements’ with preemptive force sufficient to bar common-law claims unless EPA has taken a specific, lawfully authoritative action forbidding the very warning the plaintiff says was required. Relatedly, he challenges the idea that EPA’s views (especially if expressed through less-than-formal processes) can displace state-law remedies without clear congressional delegation—an argument sharpened by the post–Loper Bright environment. On impossibility, Durnell maintains Monsanto could have sought EPA approval for stronger warnings and that FIFRA contemplates label changes consistent with FIFRA, so compliance with both regimes was not truly impossible.
key_precedents: Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. v. Albrecht

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that, post–Loper Bright, we cannot let informal EPA “views” do preemptive work, and Wyeth/Albrecht’s “clear evidence” standard cautions against converting agency inaction into impossibility. But my vote rests on the statute as applied through Bates: a common-law verdict is a state “requirement,” and it survives only if it is genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding/labeling requirements; where the theory of liability turns on the absence of a specific cancer warning that EPA’s approval/misbranding framework has not required (and has treated as potentially misleading), the state duty functions as “additional or different” under § 136v(b). Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s framing sharpens the narrow ground: we need not defer to EPA’s policy pronouncements, only recognize that Congress made the EPA-approved label the operative federal baseline such that a jury mandate for different label content cannot be called “parallel” in operation. I would keep the holding tightly limited to cases where state liability would compel a warning that cannot be added to the EPA-approved label without prior federal approval and would contradict the federal label-approval/misbranding determination on the same warning.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point—that EPA approval and related statements may not always be a freestanding, binding federal “requirement,” especially post–Loper Bright—does not defeat preemption here because the operative constraint comes from FIFRA’s enacted text, which makes the EPA-approved label the lawful baseline and forbids sale with labeling that departs from it. Under Bates, a state common-law verdict is itself a “requirement,” and it survives only if it is genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding standard; where EPA has approved a label omitting a cancer warning and has indicated that such a warning would be misleading, the Missouri duty necessarily compels different label content, not merely parallel enforcement of federal misbranding. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito correctly reframe this as a textual conflict with § 136v(b)’s “in addition to or different from” language rather than deference to informal agency views. Wyeth/Albrecht “clear evidence” arguments about whether Monsanto might have asked for a different label do not answer the express-preemption question when liability turns on requiring label language that federal law does not permit absent EPA approval and that the federal scheme has already rejected as inconsistent with its misbranding/approval structure.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that under Wyeth/Albrecht there is no “clear evidence” EPA would have rejected a strengthened warning, and that informal agency views should not become freestanding preemptive commands—does not overcome the express-preemption problem under § 136v(b). As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, Bates treats common-law verdicts as state “requirements,” and the only safe harbor is a genuinely parallel misbranding theory; a verdict premised on the absence of a glyphosate cancer warning is not “equivalent” to FIFRA where EPA has approved a label omitting that warning within a scheme that makes false or misleading warnings unlawful. Even if Monsanto could ask EPA for a change, FIFRA does not allow it to implement the jury-demanded warning unilaterally, so the state duty operates as an “additional or different” labeling requirement that Congress barred to preserve national uniformity. Accordingly, I remain with petitioner on statutory text and structure, without resting on deference to EPA’s informal preemption views.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s uniformity point seriously: a tort verdict can function as a de facto labeling mandate and § 136v(b) reaches common-law “requirements.” But Bates makes the dispositive question whether the state duty is genuinely non-parallel to FIFRA’s own misbranding standard, not whether EPA once approved a label omitting a warning; absent a lawfully binding EPA action specifically barring this warning, EPA’s repeated “misleading” characterizations look more like persuasive agency views than a federal “requirement” that flips a parallel misbranding theory into an “additional or different” one. Justice Alito’s Mensing-style impossibility framing also doesn’t land for me because Wyeth/Albrecht require clear evidence the agency would have rejected the change, and the record described (general EPA opposition rather than a concrete denial) does not show Monsanto lacked a lawful pathway to seek approval for strengthened language consistent with FIFRA. Given FIFRA’s limited express-preemption text and the traditional role of state compensation remedies for injured people, I would not expand § 136v(b) to treat nonbinding agency positions and prior approvals as categorically extinguishing a Bates-preserved parallel claim.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that, under Wyeth/Albrecht, we should hesitate to find preemption absent “clear evidence” EPA would have rejected this warning, and post–Loper Bright we should not let informal agency views do preemptive work. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett frame it, the dispositive analysis is express preemption under § 136v(b) and Bates’s “genuinely equivalent” requirement: a state verdict that turns on adding a glyphosate cancer warning is not parallel if, in operation, it compels label content that the federal label-approval/misbranding regime has already treated as unwarranted and potentially misleading. Even without deference to EPA’s policy pronouncements, FIFRA’s structure makes the EPA-approved label the operative baseline and forbids unapproved labeling changes, so the state duty functions as an “additional or different” labeling requirement rather than mere enforcement of FIFRA’s misbranding standard. I would keep the holding narrow to records like this one, where the state theory necessarily demands the very warning the federal scheme has effectively rejected, preserving Bates’s space for truly parallel misbranding claims.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor make the best point that EPA registration and informal agency views, standing alone—especially post–Loper Bright—should not be treated as freestanding, preemptive commands, and they invoke Wyeth/Albrecht’s “clear evidence” rubric to argue Monsanto might have sought approval for a stronger warning. But even granting that, Bates already instructs that common-law verdicts are “requirements,” and they survive only if they are genuinely parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding standard; a verdict that necessarily turns on the absence of a cancer warning after EPA has approved a label without one (and where adding the warning risks making the label “false or misleading” under FIFRA) is not “parallel” in operation, it is “in addition to or different from” under § 136v(b). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the most legally defensible ground is statutory text applied through Bates, not deference to agency say-so: the state duty here functions as a relabeling mandate that displaces the federally operative label-approval/misbranding framework. Albrecht’s “clear evidence” is therefore at most confirmatory on implied preemption and does not undo the express-preemption problem where state liability depends on different label content than the federal regime allows absent EPA approval.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor make the best point that EPA registration and related agency views may not themselves be a freestanding, binding federal “requirement,” and that Wyeth/Albrecht demand “clear evidence” for impossibility. But I agree with the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s framing that we do not need to rest on deference to informal EPA pronouncements: under Bates, a tort verdict is a state “requirement for labeling,” and it is preempted by § 136v(b) when it effectively compels label language that is “in addition to or different from” the federally operative label-approval/misbranding regime. Where, as here, EPA has approved a label omitting the cancer warning and has concluded that such a warning would be misleading under FIFRA’s misbranding framework, the state duty is not genuinely “parallel” in operation—it substitutes a jury’s labeling judgment for the federal one, defeating national uniformity Congress designed. Albrecht’s “clear evidence” lens remains relevant to implied preemption, but it does not negate the textual express-preemption problem when the only path to liability is a different label than federal law allows absent EPA approval.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson correctly emphasize that post–Loper Bright we should not treat EPA’s informal views as freestanding preemptive “requirements,” and that Wyeth/Albrecht demands rigor before finding impossibility. But my conclusion rests on the statute’s text as applied through Bates: the Missouri verdict functions as a state “requirement for labeling” that is “in addition to or different from” the federally operative label-approval/misbranding scheme because liability turns on the absence of a warning the federal regime has affirmatively not required on the approved label. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, the surviving space under Bates is for truly parallel misbranding claims; a jury mandate to add a specific cancer warning after EPA has approved a label without it (within a system that makes unapproved or misleading labeling unlawful) is not equivalent in operation, even if Monsanto could have petitioned EPA. On this record, Albrecht-style “clear evidence” is not the dispositive frame because the express-preemption inquiry asks whether the state duty compels different label content than federal law makes operative, and here it does.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that, under Bates, a common-law verdict can operate as a state “requirement for labeling” and will be preempted if it is truly “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s operative standard. But their analysis assumes that EPA’s approval of a label omitting a cancer warning (plus EPA’s repeated view that such a warning would be “misleading”) is itself the kind of specific federal requirement that makes the state duty necessarily contradictory, rather than potentially parallel to FIFRA’s own misbranding prohibition; post–Loper Bright, I am reluctant to treat generalized agency positions as dispositive without a concrete, lawfully binding federal denial forbidding the warning. Justice Alito’s and Justice Gorsuch’s “no unilateral change” framing sounds in Mensing-style impossibility, yet Wyeth/Albrecht require clear evidence that the agency would have rejected the precise warning, and I do not see that level of formal agency action in this record. On my view, the presumption against displacing state remedial schemes and Bates’s preserved space for parallel misbranding claims counsel against categorical preemption here, absent a clearer federal command.

Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, common-law claims survive only to the extent they impose “parallel” duties genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding standard; where EPA has affirmatively determined a cancer warning is not required and would render the label false or misleading, the state duty is not parallel but conflicting. Given FIFRA’s scheme requiring EPA approval for label changes and treating unapproved or misleading warnings as misbranding, the verdict also triggers conflict (impossibility/obstacle) preemption in the manner of PLIVA, Inc. v. Mensing and Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. v. Albrecht—courts should not allow juries to displace a federal labeling judgment. A narrow ruling enforcing § 136v(b) on these facts best preserves national uniformity and institutional legitimacy while respecting Bates’s preserved space for truly equivalent state-law misbranding claims.

Under Bates v. Samuel Alito.reasoning: FIFRA expressly preempts this verdict because it imposes a state-law “requirement for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), by demanding a cancer warning that EPA has repeatedly found unwarranted and, in EPA’s view, misleading and therefore misbranding under FIFRA’s label-approval scheme. Under Bates, a state duty survives only if it is “genuinely equivalent” to FIFRA’s misbranding standard; where EPA has affirmatively concluded that the very warning at issue should not appear, the state requirement is not “parallel” in fact but contradictory. Impossibility preemption also applies because a registrant cannot unilaterally add or materially change hazard warnings without EPA approval, and federal law cannot be satisfied simultaneously with a state verdict compelling the warning, consistent with Mensing and Albrecht’s focus on whether federal law permits the demanded label change. Allowing juries to override EPA’s labeling determinations would undermine FIFRA’s national-uniformity objective and convert tort verdicts into de facto labeling regulation contrary to the statute’s text.

Dow Agrosciences, state failure-to-warn verdicts survive where they plausibly parallel FIFRA’s own misbranding standard rather than create a novel labeling regime. Here, EPA has repeatedly concluded (through the registration/label-approval scheme Congress created) that a glyphosate cancer warning is not required and would be misleading/misbranding, so a state-law verdict compelling that warning is not parallel to FIFRA but instead contradicts the federal labeling judgment and imposes an additional/different label requirement. That contradiction also creates an impossibility-style conflict in practice because FIFRA does not permit a registrant to unilaterally add a new hazard warning without EPA approval, making it unrealistic to treat the state duty as merely enforcing the same federal standard (cf. Given FIFRA’s “Uniformity” design and the statutory coherence concerns emphasized in Bates, the failure-to-warn verdict is preempted.

Post–Loper Bright, EPA’s views do not expand FIFRA’s preemptive scope, but the statute’s text and Bates’s framework suffice to preempt a jury-imposed label requirement that diverges from the federally approved labeling determination.

Dow Agrosciences, a tort claim survives only if it is genuinely “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding standard—i.e., liability would attach under state law only where the label is also misbranded under FIFRA; but where EPA has affirmatively determined a cancer warning is not required (and would be false or misleading), the state duty cannot be “equivalent” to federal law. As an institutional matter, preserving FIFRA’s uniform national labeling regime and avoiding jury-by-jury relabeling of EPA-registered products fits the statutory design and promotes administrable, predictable rules.

The text of § 136v(b), read against FIFRA’s integrated registration and misbranding framework, points to preemption where a state tort verdict effectively substitutes a jury’s labeling judgment for EPA’s.
